title: Italy's student and cost-of-living protests
dek: Students and cost-of-living protesters march against Giorgia Meloni's government, the clashes with police in Turin, Milan and Bologna, and the unions' call for a general strike.
summary: On Friday, October 16, students marched in dozens of Italian cities on what organisers called "No Meloni Day", protesting run-down schools, a decree capping foreign pupils at 30% of a class, the cost of living and military spending. Organisers say more than 400,000 took part; the Education Ministry puts participation in the school strike at about 1%. Police used water cannon and tear gas in Turin, and bottles and firecrackers were thrown at police in Rome.

On Saturday, October 17, cost-of-living marches called by the "Italia in Piazza" movement were held in several cities. In Milan, groups broke away and clashed with police around Piazza Duomo; Il Giorno, citing police and the prefecture, reports about 50 people detained and 15 officers injured. In Rome, the CGIL union held a separate rally and announced a general strike for November 20.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the right to protest does not mean turning cities into battlefields. Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara calls the violence political hooliganism. Students and unions say the protests are about schools, wages and prices, with inflation at 4.2% in September according to Istat. Italy holds a general election next year.

phases.name: Cost-of-living marches and the CGIL rally

events.label: reported
events.text: Farmers and truck drivers block roads in Puglia, Calabria and Sicily during the week over fuel prices, and students camp out in Milan, Rome and Bologna, AFP reports. Istat puts September inflation at 4.2%, mainly because of fuel prices.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Students march in dozens of cities on "No Meloni Day", against run-down schools, the school decree, the cost of living and military spending. Schools are occupied in several cities.

events.label: reported
events.text: Organisers say more than 400,000 young people took part, La Repubblica reports; provisional Education Ministry figures put participation in the school strike at 1.08%, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Turin, protesters throw stones and other objects at police in Piazza Castello, and police respond with water cannon and tear gas.

events.label: reported
events.text: Avvenire reports that 10 officers were injured in Turin, three minors were arrested for resisting a public official and about 50 others were identified and referred to judicial authorities.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Rome, thousands rally outside the Education Ministry; police say bottles, flares and firecrackers are thrown at officers.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Verona, police identify 21 young people and report them over criminal damage and other offences; Il Sole 24 Ore says 20 of them are under 18. Clashes are also reported in Bologna.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Meloni says she welcomes mobilisation but condemns the violence and attacks on police, and calls on all parties to back peaceful protest. Education Minister Valditara calls the violence political hooliganism, not democratic dissent.

events.label: reported
events.text: Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi says police acted decisively, professionally and prudently on a difficult day, La Repubblica reports. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini calls students who threw stones criminals, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Cost-of-living marches called by the "Italia in Piazza" movement, which began on social media, are held in several cities, including Milan and Bologna; Open also lists Turin, Florence, Rome, Naples and Genoa.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Milan, groups break away from the march and clash with police around Piazza Duomo and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. Police use tear gas and a water cannon after stones and other objects are thrown; shops close and the Duomo metro station is shut.

events.label: reported
events.text: Il Giorno, citing a preliminary police and prefecture report, says about 50 people were detained in Milan, almost half of them minors, and 15 members of the security forces were injured. Sky TG24 reports five young people taken to hospital with injuries first described as minor.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Bologna, police use a water cannon after clashes near the railway station and make seven arrests, Reuters reports citing ANSA.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Rome, the CGIL union and more than 100 associations march from Piazza della Repubblica to Piazza del Popolo. CGIL leader Maurizio Landini announces a general strike for November 20 and says more than 100,000 people took part; no independent count has been published.

events.label: reported
events.text: Opposition leaders Elly Schlein (PD) and Giuseppe Conte (M5S) attend the CGIL rally; Conte calls for the government to step down, Sky TG24 reports.

events.label: pending
events.text: General strike called by the CGIL for November 20. Further protests, final arrest and injury figures for October 16 and 17, and any government response to the protesters' demands are still being checked.

claims.title: What are the protests about?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: The government condemns the violence. Meloni says she welcomes peaceful mobilisation; Valditara calls the violence political hooliganism with nothing to do with students' rights, and Tajani accuses part of the opposition of fuelling the unrest.
claims.b: Students and unions say the protests are about crumbling schools, the school decree, low wages, rising prices and military spending. The CGIL says Italy is in a dramatic economic and social crisis.
claims.status: Open. Both positions are on record.

claims.title: How many took part on October 16?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: Organisers say more than 400,000 young people marched.
claims.b: Provisional Education Ministry figures put participation in the school strike at 1.08%.
claims.status: The two figures measure different things (marchers and striking school staff and students), and no independent count of marchers has been published.
